The salt had long since turned Elias Thorne's knuckles into maps of the sea, each crease a chart of a storm he had weathered. For forty-two years, he had kept the Blackwood Point Lighthouse, a granite tooth jutting out of the Atlantic where the coast turned sharp and unforgiving. The light rotated above him, a rhythmic blink that marked the hours for every ship within twenty miles, and for Elias, it marked the silence.

It was November 14th, 1924, when the gale hit. The wind screamed through the gallery railings, a sound like a freight train passing through a tunnel, and the sea churned below, white-capped and violent. Elias had secured the lantern room and was descending the spiral stairs when a heavy thud came from the lower cove, the rocky shelf where the keeper's small skiff was usually moored.

He grabbed his oilskin coat and the oil lamp, stepping out into the gale. The lantern's beam swept the water, cutting through the rain. There, caught in the jagged teeth of the rocks, was a bottle. It was dark glass, thick and old, sealed with a cork that had held firm against the salt and the pressure. It had washed up at the base of the cove, wedged between two boulders that usually stood dry.

Elias hauled himself down the slippery rocks, his boots finding purchase only by inches. He grabbed the bottle, his heart hammering against his ribs, and scrambled back up to the skiff's berth, where he finally could breathe. The bottle was warm in his grip, strangely so, as if the sea had heated it. He wiped the seawater from the glass and held it to the lamp's flame.

Inside, a scroll of paper was tightly rolled. It was not the kind of message a sailor left when a ship was sinking. The paper was thick, cream-colored, and smelled of lavender and old ink. Elias took it to the kitchen table, dried it over the stove, and unrolled it with trembling fingers.

The handwriting was elegant, looping and precise.

*To the Keeper of Blackwood Point,*
*If you are reading this, the tide has turned, and I have failed to make the shore in time. My name is Clara Vane. I am a cartographer for the Royal Navy, and I have been mapping the shoals off this coast for three years. Below the surface of the Blackwood shoals, there is a trench I could not measure. It is deeper than any chart, and it shifts. I have marked its location on the attached map, but the paper may have rotted. I am sending this in the hope that the light at Blackwood will never be extinguished. If it is, the ships will follow my false lines into the dark. Do not trust the depth readings from the last winter. They are wrong.*
*Clara Vane*
*November 10th, 1924*

Elias read it three times. November 10th. Four days ago. He looked at the date on his own logbook, November 14th. Four days, and she had been lost to the sea.

He turned the bottle over. Taped to the inside of the glass was a small square of paper, the map she had mentioned. It showed the coastline of Blackwood Point, the lighthouse, and the shoals. Where the charts showed a steady slope to the water, a jagged red line cut through the blue, marking the trench. Beneath it, in smaller script: *The depth here is not what the lead line says. Trust the light.*

Elias sat back in his chair. The logbook for the last winter was open on the shelf. He had recorded the depth readings himself, every week, for the Admiralty. He had never questioned them. He had never thought to question them. He had trusted the lead line, the instrument, the routine.

He looked at the map again. The red line ran right through the channel where the *HMS Peregrine* had gone missing in January, a ship with a full crew and no survivors. The Admiralty had called it a collision with a submerged rock. Elias had never believed that. He had always thought the rock was a myth.

He picked up his pen. He had to write to the Admiralty. He had to tell them about the trench, about Clara Vane, about the readings that were wrong. He wrote the letter by hand, his handwriting shaky but clear. He sealed it in an envelope, addressed it to the Director of Naval Hydrography in London, and placed it in a waterproof tin.

Then he went up to the lantern room. The gale was still howling, but the light was steady. He lit the kerosene lamp, checked the wick, and turned the lens. The beam swept the dark water, cutting through the rain, the fog, the night.

He sat at the desk in the lantern room and wrote in his logbook.

*November 14th, 1924. A message in a bottle found at the base of the cove. The sender, Clara Vane, cartographer, is presumed lost. Her map shows a trench on the Blackwood shoals that contradicts all previous readings. I have sent a report to the Admiralty. I will not change the light's schedule. I will not change the readings. I will keep the light burning, and I will watch the water.*

He closed the logbook. The light turned, sweeping the dark, the beam cutting through the rain, the fog, the night. It was a small light, a single point of fire in the vast dark, but it was enough. It was enough for the *HMS Peregrine*, and it was enough for the ships that would come after.

The wind howled, and the sea crashed against the rocks. Elias sat in the warm glow of the lantern room, listening to the light turn, and he felt, for the first time in forty-two years, that he was not alone. The sea had spoken, and he had heard it. He had written it down, and he would keep it written.

The bottle sat on the desk, empty now, the cork still sealed tight. It had traveled thousands of miles to reach him. It had traveled through storms and silence, through the dark and the cold, to tell him the truth. And he would tell it to the world.

He looked out the window. The light was still turning, steady and true. The trench was still there, hidden beneath the waves. But the light was on. That was enough. That was everything.

The next morning, the sun rose over the Blackwood Point. The sea was calm, the water a deep blue, and the light at the top of the tower was still turning, sweeping the horizon, the beam cutting through the morning mist. Elias Thorne sat at his desk, writing in his logbook, his pen moving across the page, the map of the trench folded in his pocket. He would send the letter today. He would send it by the next ship that came in.

And the light would keep turning.

The wind at Blackwood Point did not howl; it scoured. For thirty-four years, Elias Thorne had watched it scour the granite of the tower, stripping the paint from the gallery railing and whispering through the cracks in the masonry. He was a man of the same texture, weathered and unyielding, with hands that smelled perpetually of kerosene and salt.

It was November 14, 1924, a Tuesday of gray drizzle and bruising clouds, when the bottle came in. Elias had finished his evening round, checking the great Fresnel lens and polishing the brass fittings until they caught the dim light of the oil lamp. He was descending the iron spiral stairs when the sound came, a soft, rhythmic thumping against the base of the tower, followed by the splash of water retreating over the jagged rocks below.

He went to the gallery, his oilskin coat heavy on his shoulders. There, caught in a tangle of seaweed half-buried in the sand at the foot of the cliff, lay a bottle of thick, green glass. It had survived the storm, or perhaps it had been thrown in at the exact moment the tide turned, for the surf had not yet claimed it.

Elias waded out, the cold water biting through his boots, and retrieved it. The cork was still sealed, though the water had softened the wax. He carried it back to the warmth of the lantern room, dried it on his coat, and set it on the small oak table beside the logbook.

The date was stamped on the inside of the cork: *October 3, 1924*. It had traveled three weeks across the North Atlantic. Elias uncorked it with a pocket knife, the wood giving way with a wet pop. He unrolled the paper inside. It was thin, fragile, and written in ink that had faded to the color of a bruise.

*To whoever finds this, or to the sea itself:*

*My name is Arthur Penhaligon, and I am writing this from the deck of the merchant vessel HMS *Aethelgard*. We are lost. The compass has failed, spinning uselessly in its housing, and the stars are hidden behind a wall of fog that has not lifted since the 28th of September. We have three days of water and little food. I know the coast is near; I can hear the breakers, though I cannot see them. If you are a keeper, or a fisherman, or a ghost, please know that we are here. We are not dead yet. We are waiting for the light.*

*Signed, Arthur Penhaligon, First Mate.*

Elias read the note twice. The date of the entry, the 28th of September, was nearly two weeks prior to the date of the bottle's discovery. The *Aethelgard* had been sailing these waters for a fortnight, blind and drifting, while the light at Blackwood Point had burned steadily, night after night, guiding no one.

He looked at the logbook. Every night since the 28th of September, the light had turned. He checked the entry for the 28th. *Fog thick. Light burning. No vessels reported.* He checked the 29th, the 30th, and every night since. The log showed a perfect record of a light that had never been seen.

Elias walked to the window. The fog had lifted for a moment, revealing the dark water churning against the rocks, but the sea was empty. No ship's lantern, no smoke, no silhouette against the gray sky.

He sat back down and picked up his pen. He could not leave the tower. The rotation mechanism required his hand every hour on the hour to ensure the lens did not seize, and a keeper who left his post was a dead keeper, or worse, a keeper whose station went dark. But he did not have to stay silent.

He wrote in the margin of the logbook, in his own steady hand: *November 14, 1924. Message received from Arthur Penhaligon, First Mate of the HMS Aethelgard. Vessel lost, compass failed, last known position estimated three miles east of the point. Light has been burning since September 28. No ship sighted. Writing reply.*

He took a fresh sheet of paper from his desk and wrote a response. He did not know the coordinates of the ship, for he had no way of knowing them, but he knew the coast. He knew the shoals, the hidden reefs, and the exact angle at which the light cut through the fog.

*Mr. Penhaligon,*

*Your message reached Blackwood Point on November 14, 1924. I am the keeper, Elias Thorne. The light has been burning every night since the 28th of September. I do not know why you did not see it. Perhaps the fog was too thick, or perhaps the light was not enough for the distance. I cannot move the tower. I cannot send a boat in this weather. But I can tell you where the shoals are.*

*If you are still at sea, steer west. The light is the only constant you have. If you are on land, look for the white tower on the cliff. Do not trust the compass. Trust the light.*

*Elias Thorne, Keeper, Blackwood Point.*

Elias rolled the paper tight, tied it with a piece of twine from his pocket, and placed it in the green bottle. He did not have a cork for the new message, so he used a piece of wax from the lamp stand to seal the neck. He walked back out to the gallery. The wind had picked up again, driving the rain sideways.

He thought about the *Aethelgard*. If they were still out there, three weeks of drifting would have left them weak. They might have been rescued by another ship, or they might have been stranded on an island he had never heard of. Or they might have never been lost at all, and the ship had found its way in by some miracle. The message had been a hope, cast into the dark, and it had traveled three weeks to reach him.

He held the bottle over the churning water. He could not throw it back into the sea with the same confidence he had held when he picked it up. It was a message to the past, or to a ship that might be gone. But it was the only thing he had.

He threw it as hard as he could, aiming for the open water beyond the breakers, where the tide would carry it west. The bottle hit the water with a sharp splash and vanished into the gray.

Elias stood at the railing for a long time, watching the spot where it had gone. The fog began to roll back in, thick and white, swallowing the sea. He turned back to the tower, climbed the iron stairs, and checked the logbook one last time before lighting the lamp for the night.

*November 14, 1924. Reply sent. Waiting for a response that may never come. Light burning as usual.*

He wound the mechanism, the gears turning with their familiar, rhythmic groan. The great lens began to rotate, cutting a beam through the dark, sweeping the empty sea, searching for a ship that might never answer.

Start by building a wedding budget from the top down. Look at what you can afford each month for a loan payment, not just what you want the day to cost. A good rule of thumb: total wedding debt plus other monthly debt payments shouldn't exceed about 36% of your take-home pay. Then get quotes from a few places. Ask family and friends if they'd contribute in other ways, like help with planning or a small gift instead of cash. Some couples also set up a cash registry or a honeymoon fund alongside traditional gifts.

Before you sign, think about what your marriage starts with. Many financial planners suggest entering marriage with as little debt as possible, since new households often face other costs right away. A wedding loan can be a reasonable choice, but it depends on your income, the loan terms, and how much debt you'd be carrying into your marriage. Here's how to think it through.

Where a loan makes sense
- You have a stable income and can afford the monthly payment without stretching your budget.
- The loan has a low interest rate and a short term, so you pay it off before any big financial changes (like a baby or moving).
- The cost of borrowing is small compared with the value of the day. For example, a $5,000 loan at 8% over two years costs roughly $430 in interest.
- You'd otherwise be using high-interest credit cards.

Where it usually doesn't
- You'd be borrowing more than you can comfortably repay alongside other debts.
- The rate is high, or the term is long enough that you'd be paying for the wedding for years.
- You'd be borrowing on the promise of a future income that isn't secured yet.

A few things to consider
- Your parents' inability to help isn't a reason to borrow. It just means the budget falls on you, so the numbers need to work on your own.
- A wedding is one of the few large expenses where the return is emotional, not financial. That's a valid reason to spend, but it's also why it's easy to overspend.
- Some couples save for part of it and borrow the rest, or choose a smaller guest list, a different venue, or a date in the off-season to cut costs.

Gardez tout le dépôt pour un mur éraflé après quatre ans ? Cela dépend du contrat que vous avez signé et de votre pays, mais en règle générale, cette demande semble excessive. Un locataire ne peut pas être tenu responsable de l'usure normale du logement. Une éraflure légère, qui s'explique par l'usage normal, ne justifie pas normalement le prélèvement intégral du dépôt. On peut généralement exiger qu'on remette le logement dans l'état où il se trouvait au départ, sauf dépréciation due au temps.

Voici ce que je vous conseille de faire :

1. **Relisez votre bail et l'état des lieux de départ.** Cherchez les clauses sur le dépôt, l'usure normale et les réparations. Comparez avec les photos et les notes de l'état des lieux d'entrée.
2. **Rassemblez les preuves.** Photos du mur avant votre départ, copies du bail et de l'état des lieux, toutes les correspondances avec votre propriétaire (mails, messages, lettres).
3. **Répondez par écrit au propriétaire.** Dites-lui poliment que vous contestez la retenue intégrale, exposez les faits (quatre ans d'occupation, éraflure mineure), et proposez un règlement raisonnable, par exemple le coût réel d'une simple retouche de peinture. Exigez un détail écrit des frais s'il veut garder une partie.
4. **Si le propriétaire refuse**, cherchez l'aide d'une association de locataires ou d'un syndicat de votre ville. Dans de nombreux pays, il existe aussi un médiateur ou un tribunal de petite créance pour régler ce genre de litige.

Avant tout, j'aimerais savoir dans quel pays et quelle ville vous louez, ainsi que ce qui est écrit dans votre bail concernant le dépôt et l'usure normale. Cela me permettra de vous donner des informations plus précises.

En France, un propriétaire ne peut pas garder la totalité de votre dépôt de garantie pour un seul mur égratigné après quatre années de bonne occupation. La loi considère que l'usure normale du logement, qui inclut de légères marques sur les murs, est à sa charge. Il ne peut réclamer des sommes qu'en cas de dégâts avérés et excédant cette usure normale, et il doit pouvoir les justifier.

Voici ce que je vous conseille de faire :

1. **Rassemblez les preuves.** Relisez votre état des lieux d'entrée et de sortie. Si vous avez des photos ou des échanges écrits (messages, courriels) montrant l'état du mur à l'arrivée ou lors d'un état intermédiaire, conservez-les. C'est l'élément le plus important.
2. **Demandez un devis ou une facture.** Si le propriétaire souhaite faire repeindre le mur, il doit vous fournir un devis ou une facture détaillée. Il ne peut pas retenir une somme arbitraire.
3. **Répondez par écrit.** Envoyez-lui un courriel ou une lettre recommandée avec accusé de réception. Expliquez poliment qu'il ne peut pas retenir la totalité du dépôt pour une usure normale, et proposez-lui de ne payer que le coût réel de la remise en état, s'il y en a vraiment une.
4. **Sachez qu'il y a des délais.** En général, le propriétaire doit vous rendre le dépôt dans un délai raisonnable après la restitution des clés (souvent quelques semaines), avec un éventuel décompte écrit en cas de retenue. S'il ne le fait pas, vous pouvez le relancer officiellement.
5. **En cas de blocage**, vous pouvez saisir le médiateur de l'immobilier, le juge d'instance, ou consulter une association de locataires (comme la CLAJ ou une permanence juridique locale). Je peux aussi vous aider à rédiger la lettre de réclamation si vous me donnez quelques détails.

- ce que le propriétaire a écrit exactement pour justifier la retenue ;
- le montant du dépôt et le montant qu'il souhaite garder.

That is a much grayer area than the English level, and the answer depends heavily on **how you say it** and **what the job requires**.

**Where it usually goes wrong:**
If your title on every contract and pay slip was "Team Member," but you write "Project Lead" in the title line of your CV, a recruiter checking your employment history will see a mismatch. If the role is senior and they assume you have managed budgets, hired people and been held accountable for delivery, they have hired you for a job you haven't done. That is a real risk, and it can cost you at the first reference check.

**Where it can be honest:**
In many companies, titles are not standardized. "Team Member" may have been the HR label while your actual work was leading the project. If that's true, you can write:

> **Project Lead** (Team Member with project leadership responsibilities)  
> *Led weekly client meetings, coordinated the delivery schedule, and reported directly to the programme manager.*

This states the truth clearly: the official title, and what you actually did. Recruiters care more about what you did than the label.

**A simple test:**
Ask yourself: if someone asked "What did a Project Lead do in your company?", would your answer describe *leading* or *helping out*? If it's the former, you're fine. If it's the latter, lead with the work and let the official title sit in the footnotes.

That's a different situation from the English level, and the answer is more nuanced.

If your official job title on your contract or payslip was **Project Lead** (or Project Manager, Team Lead, etc.), then using that title on your CV is accurate, even if some of your daily work felt like a team member's. Companies often give senior-sounding titles to people who lead small teams or specific workstreams. In that case, you're not misrepresenting anything.

Where it becomes misleading is if your official title was **Team Member** and you're changing it to **Project Lead** on your CV to make it sound more senior. That can backfire:

- Background checks often verify the official job title.
- In an interview, someone might ask: "What did 'lead' mean in your role?" If you can't show that you led people, budgets, timelines or decisions, it looks like an exaggeration.
- If you get the job and then can't deliver on the "lead" part, you're in a weaker position from day one.

However, you can describe the work truthfully without changing the title. For example:

- **Team Member, [Company]** (2020–2023)  
  *Led weekly team meetings, coordinated the project timeline, and reported progress to the project manager.*

Or, if you want to show leadership without claiming the title:

- **Project Team Member (co-ordinated meetings and timeline)**  
  *Facilitated weekly stand-ups, tracked deliverables, and helped the project manager make key decisions.*

The key question is: did you actually lead anything? Did you set deadlines, assign work, make decisions, or report to a manager on behalf of the team? If yes, you can describe that leadership clearly. If no, it's better to describe the coordination work honestly.

You can also think about your next role. If you want to be a Project Lead, the best path is to take on real lead responsibilities now, even in a smaller capacity, and list them as experience.
